source.title: How Does Label Noise Gradient Descent Improve Generalization in the Low SNR Regime?
source.authors: Wei Huang; Andi Han; Yu-Jin Song; Yilan Chen; Denny Wu; Difan Zou; Taiji Suzuki

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some equations and figure contents are flattened or absent, so precise figure values cannot be recovered.
record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization in low-SNR signal-noise settings, including synthetic data and modified image datasets, extending the generalization question to a setting and training modification not covered by the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper compares standard GD with label-noise GD and reports training and test outcomes. The label-noise intervention is not one of the listed versions; cited prior-work results are not recorded as rows. Figure-only numerical values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether injecting label noise improves generalization under low SNR, which is outside V1–V8. It does not compare fixed random labels with natural labels, vary width or batch size, compare convolutional and fully connected networks or adaptive optimizers, intervene on dropout, measure magnitude-aware sharpness, or remove memorized examples. Its own results therefore test none of the listed versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that label noise GD controls noise memorization while allowing signal learning, improving generalization where standard GD overfits under low SNR. The proof is restricted to a two-layer convolutional network with squared ReLU and an idealized data model; experiments provide broader qualitative evidence.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies label-flipping noise injected into gradient updates and compares it with standard GD. It does not reproduce the methods in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the performance gap between label noise GD and standard GD becomes more significant as SNR decreases; it also reports higher label-noise-GD test accuracy across tested modified-MNIST noise and signal-normalization configurations, without numerical values in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the theoretical assumptions, standard GD reaches logistic training loss at most ε with population classification error at least 0.24. Label noise GD has constant-order training loss and population error bounded by 2 exp(−Cd/n²), at its specified stopping time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Resampling label flips during training can suppress harmful input-noise memorization and improve generalization in a low-SNR signal-noise model.

fits_no_version.finding: VGG-16 with label noise GD has higher test accuracy than standard GD across tested Fourier-noise levels on a CIFAR-10 subset, with a larger gap at lower SNR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label noise GD can improve image-classification accuracy when high-frequency input noise reduces SNR.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic, deeper-network, and modified-CIFAR experiments report improved generalization with label noise GD. The individual modified-MNIST experiment is described only as consistent with the theory.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label noise GD's benefits extend across several synthetic and modified-image settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix G reports higher modified-MNIST accuracy across noise levels 4–8 and normalization values 60–140, and qualitative benefits with additional label-noise distributions and polynomial ReLU activations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The reported label-noise-GD advantage persists across tested input parameters, noise forms, and activation choices.

record.code_released: The codebase is provided in the supplementary material; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The main theorem concerns an idealized binary signal-noise distribution and a specific two-layer convolutional network with squared ReLU. The CIFAR-10 experiment uses a subset and synthetic Fourier noise; numerical figure values and uncertainty estimates for experiments are not stated in the supplied text. The paper does not test arbitrary-label memorization.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted. Other appendix results are described qualitatively or shown only in figures, with no separate text-reported outcome for each noise distribution or parameter setting.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting and the paired natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers and the effects of tuning or optimizer modifications.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against other measures.
Removal of examples selected by memorization influence, retraining, and comparison with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: States refer to whether rows establish a listed version, so none-linked rows are cannot_determine rather than absent. These are mostly comparisons of the study's own method and belong under fits_no_version. Discussion of flat minima, Adam, and data parallelism supplies no direct tests of V4, V5, or V7.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fitting fixed random labels, or compare natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No fully connected image-network comparator or test of local connectivity.
No adaptive optimizer comparison or optimizer tuning study.
No batch-size comparison or fixed-epoch large-batch study.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal and retraining of memorized examples.
